topic: Why Car Crashes Feel Like Slow Motion — Even Though Your Eyes Never Speed Up
visual_mode_reason: Combines the sunlit outdoor 150-foot Dallas SCAD free-fall tower and rapid-flashing LED wrist chronometer with 3D brain cutaways contrasting normal-frame-rate primary visual cortex against hyper-dense amygdala-hippocampal memory recording.
setup_18w: Volunteers fell backward a hundred and fifty feet off a tower while reading a flashing wrist number.

primary_case.title: David Eagleman & Chess Stetson's 2007 150-Foot Free-Fall Tower Perceptual Chronometer Test
primary_case.place: Zero Gravity Thrill Park (150-Foot SCAD Tower, Dallas, Texas) & Baylor College of Medicine / Caltech, USA
primary_case.summary: To test whether human vision genuinely speeds up like a high-speed camera during mortal terror, Chess Stetson, Matthew Fiesta, and David Eagleman strapped a rapid-flickering LED wrist chronometer onto volunteers and dropped them 150 feet backward into a net — proving eyes gain 0% extra speed while amygdala-charged memory stretches remembered time by 36%.

people.name: David M. Eagleman, Chess Stetson & Matthew P. Fiesta
people.role: Baylor College of Medicine & Caltech neuroscientists who built the wrist perceptual chronometer (PLoS ONE, 2007)
people.bio: Designed a decisive physical test separating live visual frame-rate acceleration from retrospective memory packing.

people.name: Dallas 150-Foot SCAD Free-Fall Volunteers
people.role: Healthy adults released backward unattached down a 31-meter vertical drop into a suspended catch net
people.bio: Stared at a flickering LED wrist display during ~2.5 seconds of 70-mph free fall after calibrating their ground-level visual fusion threshold.

people.name: Lila Davachi, David Clewett & Elizabeth A. Kensinger
people.role: Modern memory neuroscientists mapping hippocampal event density (2019) and negative-valence recapitulation (2018)
people.bio: Showed how high-arousal boundaries pack extra sensory snapshots into hippocampal memory, making short crises read back as long.

core_facts.fact: Nearly everyone who survives a highway spinout, ladder slip, or sudden crisis swears time physically slowed down while it happened — prompting Stetson, Fiesta & Eagleman (2007 PLoS ONE) to test whether the brain's visual camera actually speeds up its frame rate.

Eagleman's team engineered a custom wrist-mounted 'perceptual chronometer' whose LED segments alternated a two-digit number with its exact negative inverse just slightly faster than each person's ground-level flicker threshold — so on solid ground it blurred into a uniform square, and ONLY a real-time speedup in visual temporal resolution could make the digits readable.

Volunteers were hoisted 150 feet (roughly 31 meters) up a Dallas Suspended Catch Air Device (SCAD) tower, hung backward from a release hook with zero bungee cord, and dropped into ~2.5 seconds of pure free fall reaching ~70 mph before landing safely in an air-cushioned net.

Although every volunteer's actual 150-foot backward free fall lasted roughly 2.5 seconds (watching others fall served as the 100 percent reference), jumpers retrospectively estimated their own terrifying fall lasted 36 percent longer — 136 percent of a watched fall — despite 0 percent improvement in reading the flashing wrist chronometer.
During the 150-foot plunge, volunteers' accuracy at reading the fast-alternating wrist LED digits did not beat normal ground-level vision at all — ruling out Hollywood 'bullet-time' eye acceleration.

Eagleman (2008 Current Opinion in Neurobiology) explained the paradox: you do not SEE in slow motion during the crisis; instead, your terrified amygdala forces memory circuits to record a second, ultra-detailed sensory track.

Dirnberger et al. (2012 NeuroImage) confirmed on human fMRI that emotionally arousing stimuli simultaneously distort subjective duration and strengthen subsequent memory encoding via amygdala and insular recruitment.

Bowen, Kark & Kensinger (2018) and Clewett, DuBrow & Davachi (2019 Hippocampus) proved that negative arousal and sharp event boundaries pack denser sensory snapshots into hippocampal traces — so when your brain replays a dense 2.5-second file later, it assumes more clock time must have passed.

wow_facts.fact: Falling 150 feet backward at 70 mph stretched volunteers' remembered fall duration by 36 percent — yet gave them zero extra speed at reading a flashing LED watch strapped right in front of their eyes.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Shatters the lifelong intuition that human eyes enter 'super-speed' slow motion during emergencies.

wow_facts.fact: Slow-motion crisis perception is written AFTER the danger starts: your amygdala switches on high-density hippocampal recording, and your brain misreads the larger memory file size as longer elapsed time.
wow_facts.why_surprising: What feels like a live perceptual superpower is actually an instant retrospective memory illusion.

wow_facts.fact: This exact same hippocampal memory-density rule explains why childhood summers packed with first-time experiences feel endless in hindsight, whereas repetitive adult commute decades blur past in a blink (Clewett, DuBrow & Davachi, 2019).
wow_facts.why_surprising: Unites 2.5-second highway emergencies and 10-year adult aging perception under one single brain rule.

misconceptions.myth: Adrenaline speeds up your visual cortex frame rate so you see danger in real-time Matrix slow motion.
misconceptions.truth: Stetson, Fiesta & Eagleman's (2007) flashing wrist chronometer proved visual temporal resolution does not speed up during a 150-foot free fall.
misconceptions.reality: Stetson, Fiesta & Eagleman's (2007) flashing wrist chronometer proved visual temporal resolution does not speed up during a 150-foot free fall.

misconceptions.myth: People who report slow-motion car skids are exaggerating or making stories up.
misconceptions.truth: The 36% time-stretch is completely real to the survivor because amygdala-charged hippocampal traces store far more sensory detail per second than calm moments.
misconceptions.reality: The 36% time-stretch is completely real to the survivor because amygdala-charged hippocampal traces store far more sensory detail per second than calm moments.

misconceptions.myth: Years inevitably feel faster after 40 because an aging biological clock ticks slower.
misconceptions.truth: Routine autopilot starves the hippocampus of fresh event boundaries, shrinking memory file size so routine years compress on look-back.
misconceptions.reality: Routine autopilot starves the hippocampus of fresh event boundaries, shrinking memory file size so routine years compress on look-back.

everyday_hooks: Hitting highway gravel or catching a tumbling coffee mug at 50 and remembering every airborne droplet as if five full seconds passed.
Wondering why a three-second fender-bender feels longer in your memory than an entire monotonous month of identical Tuesday commutes.
Using fresh weekend routes and novel experiences after 40 to pack denser hippocampal landmarks so your years stop flying by.
